A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Gate control theory explains psychological influences on pain. [1]

items.stem: Explain the gate control theory of pain.
items.answer: Pain signals travel along small fibres to the spinal cord, where a “gate” (in the dorsal horn) controls whether they pass to the brain. Activity in large fibres (touch) and descending signals from the brain (calm, distraction) close the gate; small-fibre activity and anxiety open it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gate in spinal cord; 1 mark small/large fibres; 1 mark descending control [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the gate control theory of pain in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about explanatory power.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It led to treatments such as TENS and supports psychological pain management. Strength (explanatory power): It explains psychological effects on pain and why techniques such as distraction, rubbing and TENS reduce pain. Weakness (evidence): The physical gate mechanism has not been clearly located. Weakness (chronic pain): It does not fully explain chronic pain that persists without an obvious physical cause. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which the gate control theory explains pain better than specificity theory. In your answer, you may refer to psychological factors, reductionism and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Gate control theory explains why rubbing an injury or TENS reduces pain (large fibres close the gate). It explains psychological influences on pain, such as attention and mood, through descending signals. It can account for phantom limb pain, which specificity theory cannot. Arguments against: The exact location of the “gate” has not been identified. It does not fully explain chronic pain without injury. Specificity theory correctly identifies specialised pain receptors. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the McGill Pain Questionnaire. Include at least one point about validity.
items.answer: Strength (validity): It measures sensory, affective and evaluative qualities of pain, giving a fuller picture than a single rating. Strength (reliability): It is standardised, with the same word lists and scoring for every patient. Weakness (self-report): Patients may exaggerate or minimise pain, for example to obtain medication or to appear brave. Weakness (usefulness): It is long and requires good vocabulary, so it cannot be used with young children or some patients. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: “Psychological techniques for managing pain (attention diversion, imagery and cognitive redefinition) has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including effectiveness in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (ethics): They are non-invasive with no physical side effects or risk of addiction. items.stem: Daniel wants to find out how nurses assess pain in patients who cannot speak. Design an observation to investigate this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, the type of observation and how inter-rater reliability will be checked.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: pain behaviours; categories: grimacing, guarding, moaning, restlessness. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Nairobi, with reasons. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.

items.stem: Evaluate the McGill Pain Questionnaire in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (reliability): It is standardised, with the same word lists and scoring for every patient. Strength (validity): It measures sensory, affective and evaluative qualities of pain, giving a fuller picture than a single rating. Weakness (usefulness): It is long and requires good vocabulary, so it cannot be used with young children or some patients. Weakness (self-report): Patients may exaggerate or minimise pain, for example to obtain medication or to appear brave. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: “Psychological techniques for managing pain (attention diversion, imagery and cognitive redefinition) has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including ethics in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (long-term use): Patients learn skills they can use repeatedly without cost, which helps with chronic pain. Strength (ethics): They are non-invasive with no physical side effects or risk of addiction. Weakness (individual differences): People differ in their ability to use imagery or to concentrate, so results vary. Weakness (effectiveness): They work best for mild or moderate pain and may not help with severe acute pain. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The theory that pain is a direct response from specific pain receptors, with the amount of pain proportional to the injury”.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Specificity theory says psychological factors strongly affect pain.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain one weakness of specificity theory.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Specificity theory sees pain as a direct response to injury; gate control theory includes psychological factors. (b) It cannot explain why the same injury causes different amounts of pain in different situations, or pain without injury such as phantom limb pain, because it ignores psychological factors.

items.stem: Discuss whether the gate control theory explains pain better than specificity theory. In your answer, you may refer to usefulness and reductionism.
items.answer: Arguments for: Gate control theory explains why rubbing an injury or TENS reduces pain (large fibres close the gate). It explains psychological influences on pain, such as attention and mood, through descending signals. It can account for phantom limb pain, which specificity theory cannot. Arguments against: The exact location of the “gate” has not been identified. It does not fully explain chronic pain without injury. Specificity theory correctly identifies specialised pain receptors. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Design an observation to investigate how nurses assess pain in patients who cannot speak. Your plan must include: how inter-rater reliability will be checked, behavioural categories and ethical issues.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: pain behaviours; categories: grimacing, guarding, moaning, restlessness. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Colombo, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.answer: (a) They can be used with people who cannot report their pain (young children, people with dementia) and are less affected by self-report bias. (b) Correct. Only the person can describe their experience of pain.

items.answer: (a) Non-pain imagery or attention diversion, which shifts attention away from the pain and, according to gate control theory, closes the gate via descending signals.
